extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society / natural philosophers, observational astronomers, experimentalists, engineers, and practical miners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for observing and reporting natural-philosophy phenomena (astronomical observations, experiments on light, technical designs, and mining incidents) as exemplified in 17th‑century Philosophical Transactions reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical observation reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Record precise observational parameters (dates and exact times, altitudes, right ascension, azimuthal distances, ecliptic/longitude and latitude), the instrument used, and comparative measures to fixed stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers should give exact dates and clock-times of sightings; measure altitude and azimuthal positions (e.g. "its altitude was 4° 5': the distance of the vertical about 42° 8' from the north towards the east"); state right ascension or longitude and north/south latitude; report which fixed stars were used for distance measurements and provide repeated measurements where possible (Flamsteed's measured distances from Capella, Algol, Mirach, etc.). Note instrument details (e.g. telescope length, use of sextant), seeing conditions (clouds, twilight), and correct for refraction when stating 'true place'. Examples throughout Cassini/Hevelius/Flamsteed sections demonstrate these elements; failure to record these makes positional inferences less reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet morphology and appearance reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe size, shape and magnitude of the head (nucleus), the form of the coma, tail length, direction, brightness, and any differences between naked-eye and telescopic appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether the head is circular/oval/indented and its apparent diameter (e.g. 'almost equal to the disk of Jupiter', 'not near 1 minute diameter'); characterise the coma (broad, nearly parabolical) and tail (length in degrees, direction relative to stars and the sun, whether divided into rays). Note if tail direction deviates from being exactly opposite the sun (the text notes an angle ~10' difference). State differences observed by naked eye vs telescope and record how tail length/brightness changes with proximity to sun and twilight. These morphological notes are essential for interpreting physical nature and motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design for measuring the progressive motion of light (Rømer method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use timing of satellite emersions/immersions across different Earth–Jupiter distances (quadratures) to detect systematic retardation/advancement attributable to light's finite velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe repeated emersions/immersions of Jupiter's first satellite and compare timings when Earth is at different positions (e.g. quadratures FG vs KL); predict that if light requires time, emersions observed when Earth is farther will appear later by the light-travel delay across the added distance. Use many revolutions (not just one or two) because single revolution differences may be too small; aggregate observations over many revolutions (Rømer notes that 40 revolutions produce a sensibly detectable effect) and compute expected retardation from known geometry (satellite period ~424 hours, Earth–Jupiter distance changes measured in Earth diameters). Document the geometric setup (labelled diagram A sun, B Jupiter, C satellite, Earth positions), and publish observed timing differences and predictions (the paper explains the logic and gives example predictions and confirmations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering specification and performance reporting for pumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide labelled component descriptions, construction materials, dimensions, valve arrangements, operational mechanics, and measured performance (gallons per stroke, strokes per minute, total delivery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify parts by letter and function (body A A, valve aa, bucket BB, valve b, iron/C C C for lifting, handle EE, taper-box FF, additional bucket GG, spout II, supports KK). State suitable materials (oak, elm, deal planks), give dimensions of the device used in practice (example: 8 feet long, 1 foot 8 inches broad at top, ~8 inches at bottom), and report measured throughput (example: "threw out 8 gallons at a stroke; and 21 strokes being made in 1 minute, there was delivered about 169 gallons in each minute"). Explain design rationale such as tapering ('cannot be allowed of any other fashion than a tapering one, because the celerity of the motion in the narrowest part... would be obstructed') and note possible modifications (handle converted to horse/mill). Include construction alternatives (bored tree, basket instead of box) and justification for choices. Omitting dimensions or performance figures reduces reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine ventilation and fire‑damp detection/mitigation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise signs of fire-damp (blueish flame in crevices, rainbow-like sheen on water, hissing blasts), document circumstances when gas appears (after driving witchets, upon removal of water), and apply practical mitigation techniques (drainage, early scouting, locally chasing/weakening gas, use of wet rags, long poles with candles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report stratigraphy and drainage measures (drive a witchet to gain room and draw water); note when fresh air is lacking and fire-damp 'begins to breed' in crevices. Describe early warning signs and responses: employ a resolute man to go ahead each morning to 'chase' the damp using wetted rags and a long wand bearing burning candles (falling on belly and creeping forward), observe that the damp may quench candles or blow them out and afterwards leave ill-scented smoke. Record incidents (a collier struck by a blast), and how changes (sinking into different seams, removal of water, thickened air from breath/smoke) alter gas behavior. These operational details serve both as diagnostic criteria and as procedural mitigation; omitting them hampers understanding of risk and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for natural-history field works
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess natural‑history works by the thoroughness of local survey, reliance on personal inquiry, usefulness to natural knowledge and trade, and the potential for providing materials to other investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given where the author 'has begun to execute this noble design by giving us a very particular account...for the most part upon his own personal inquiry.' A work is valued for advancing knowledge of nature and trade, for furnishing 'good materials' to philosophers, and for being pursued with 'care, judgment, and diligence.' Overly minute reprinting is unnecessary when the work is already well known; emphasis is on original fieldwork and utility rather than mere repetition. Use of personal observation and systematic collection of local data are key evaluation points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for naval-architecture treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge naval-architecture writing by its effort to systematise practical craft ('reduce into art'), methodological clarity, applicability for improving ship performance, and provision of quantitative notions (symmetry, weight of burden).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author is commended for attempting 'to reduce into art, as methodically as he could, a science so necessary and useful to the state' and for aiming to 'render it familiar, and to quicken those that are skilled in the mathematics and in naval architecture, to inquire after infallible ways of making ships sail better, and to find out the just weight of a ship's burden, and its true symmetry.' Evaluation emphasizes methodical presentation, practical usefulness to practitioners and the state, and stimulation of further mathematical inquiry. A mere essay/fore-runner is acceptable if it invites deeper studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for chemistry treatises aimed at practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor concise theoretical exposition that suffices to direct practical operations, comprehensive and faithful presentation of preparative methods across minerals, vegetables, and animals, and practical accessibility (translations and clear methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewed chemistry treatise is praised because it 'publishes a short and easy method for the happy attainment of all the most necessary preparations of chemistry' and 'speaks succinctly, yet seems to say so much of it as may suffice for direction to the preparations; performing his operations on minerals, vegetables, and animals.' Criteria include clarity of procedures, sufficiency of theory to guide practice, fidelity of translation (if applicable), and breadth of operative examples. Works that prioritize usable recipes and clear operations are valued over abstruse theoretical exposition alone.
